scientific_basis: Soil organic carbon is a primary substrate for soil microbial communities; higher carbon content generally supports greater microbial biomass and diversity.
Organic matter improves soil aggregate structure and porosity, increasing water-holding capacity.
Greater soil water availability buffers plants against short-term rainfall variability.
More resilient plants maintain cover through stress periods rather than dying back.
Sustained vegetation cover provides the structural base on which diverse plant communities establish.
Diverse flowering plant communities extend floral resource availability across the season, supporting a broader range of pollinator species.
Fragmentation isolates habitat patches, reducing the movement of species between them.
Connected habitat allows recolonization and gene flow, supporting higher sustained species counts.
Rainfall is the primary water input in rainfed agricultural and natural systems.
Higher temperatures increase the rate of water loss from soil and plant surfaces to the atmosphere.
Higher evapotranspiration depletes available soil water more quickly for a given rainfall input.
Water availability is a limiting resource for both flora and fauna, particularly in semi-arid systems.
Single-species plantings provide structurally uniform habitat, reducing available ecological niches relative to mixed plantings.
A wider range of habitat niches supports a wider range of species.
Broad-spectrum pesticide exposure is a well-documented pressure on pollinator populations.
Pollinators support reproduction of many flowering plant species, sustaining plant community diversity over time.
Clearing typically proceeds unevenly, leaving a fragmented mosaic of remaining forest patches.
Impervious surface expansion directly removes natural and semi-natural habitat.
Adequate soil moisture is required to sustain vegetative growth, particularly in water-limited systems.
Diverse vegetation extends flowering periods and floral resource variety available to pollinators.
Intensive agricultural management typically simplifies landscape structure relative to lower-intensity or mixed systems.
